name: Beth Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and take the routine order calls at a contact centre. I left school after secondary education and have only been on this desk a short while. I still ask someone to check a refund when the order number does not match the delivery note. The pay is low, and I do not use AI tools; the two screens we have are plenty to learn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Owen works part time unloading goods at a shop, and our children are grown and live elsewhere. We have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few similar call jobs nearby. I would like to finish working one day, but I cannot name a date from the money we have now. I like hearing a customer relax when I find the missing order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the others AI Plateau sounds like one more button for ordinary calls. I would ask to keep the paper order list until I can read the new screen without help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the calls would still be there, but I already worry about the low wage and the small amount we have saved. Owen’s part-time unloading hours change each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep answering orders and ask my colleague Mina to show me how she checks a refund on both current screens during a paid shift. In the first year of small change, I’d mend my winter coat instead of buying another and keep the cost for heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about bills, though this picture does not take away my calls. The coat can be patched; the heating bill has a date printed on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Mina catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I read the order number from the return slip instead of the delivery slip. Mina caught it before I told the customer the wrong refund amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would mend the coat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen (my partner) can sew the lining, if his hands are free after work. If he cannot, I can ask the repair shop its price before deciding; I am not counting free help as certain.

say: I’d ask to keep the **paper order list** beside my headset.
I’d say **ordinary calls** still need a person in the mild picture.
think: I think my **order shifts** continue for now.
I worry **thin savings** and low pay leave little space for a missed bill.
do: Keep **answering orders** and learn current refund checks with Mina on paid time.
Mend **winter coat** if Owen is available or repair-shop price is affordable; defer replacement and hold money for heating.
S0.quote: The coat can be patched; the heating bill has a date printed on it.
fieldNote: Her **low wage** causes concern before any large AI change.
Mina teaches the **existing screens**, not a new AI tool.
The **coat repair** depends on Owen’s availability or shop price.

steps.text: Keep answering order calls and review current refund screens with Mina on paid time
Mend coat if Owen available or shop price affordable; defer replacement and hold difference for heating

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption may take the plain order calls I am still practising. I would ask the supervisor for the paid rota in writing before believing a promise about new work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the experienced agents might keep the difficult refunds and I could lose shifts. With less than a month saved and few nearby call jobs, that would hurt quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking my assigned calls and ask for a written count of paid beginner hours. If my shifts fall in the first year simple chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid packing desk only if written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after travel; I would keep my current shift until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A promise about retraining does not pay for the week before it begins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What rota number would matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many beginners were actually paid last month and how many are on next month’s rota. A chart of answered calls would not show me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you reach the packing desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen (my partner) would check the trip to the packing site with me. A job outside the bus timetable would mean paying someone for a lift, which could erase the extra wage.

say: I’d request **written beginner hours** before trusting a new-work promise.
I’d ask how many **paid junior shifts** remain after chats move.
think: I think **experienced agents** may keep difficult refunds.
I fear **my junior shifts** could shrink with almost no savings.
do: Keep **assigned calls** and request written paid beginner hours in 2026.
Apply after cuts for **posted paid packing work** with written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours and affordable transport; keep calls until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost shifts and a paid-week gap.
S1.quote: A promise about retraining does not pay for the week before it begins.
fieldNote: She sees **routine-call cuts** as a direct junior wage risk.
The **bus timetable** determines whether packing work is affordable.
Her written-hours request is **individual**, not collective action.

steps.text: Keep assigned order calls and ask supervisor for written paid junior hours
Apply after cuts: posted packing, written bill-covering wages/hours after bus/lift costs; retain calls until signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the floor AGI by 2028 could answer nearly every order question we get. Robots around 2031 are later, but the headset could go silent first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior job could end before I learn the harder refunds. Owen’s changing shop shifts and less than a month saved would leave us short of bills very quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for a written date if order hours are to be cut and look at posted paid stockroom roles nearby. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I’d move only with a signed offer showing written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel; I would not resign for a verbal promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can ask employers what work actually exists. I need an offer on paper before I give up the wage I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in a stockroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask if a stockroom worker checks actual parcels or only a computer list. If it is only a list, thinking AI might reach it before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could family help the search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter Faye might be able to tell me which nearby shops are hiring, but I would ask rather than assume she knows. I would not expect her to pay our bills.

say: I’d ask for **written cut dates** on order shifts.
I’d say **2028 thinking AI** reaches calls before robots.
think: I think my **junior job** could end before my skills grow.
I fear **variable shop hours** and thin savings cannot bridge a gap.
do: Seek **written cut notice** and inspect posted stockroom roles in 2026.
Move after lost calls only on **signed after-travel bill-covering wages** and written weekly hours.
Ask **daughter Faye** about nearby vacancies without assuming she knows or can pay bills.
S2.quote: I need an offer on paper before I give up the wage I have.
fieldNote: Her **junior call work** is exposed in 2028.
Faye’s **job information is uncertain** and no cash support is assumed.
The new job must pay **after travel** and be written before she leaves.

steps.text: Inspect posted paid nearby stockroom roles before 2028
Move only on signed after-travel bill-covering weekly wages and hours after call loss
Ask daughter Faye whether she knows of nearby vacancies without counting on her answer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives me time to learn whether the stockroom has real paid hours. I would ask to work beside someone there before taking a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could check parcels by hand if someone showed me the labels slowly. Full thinking AI may do the stock list in 2031, with robots around 2034 taking more of the lifting later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d take a supervised paid stockroom trial only if the shop posts a paid vacancy and the lifting is safe for me. If the role requires a safety course, I’d take it only when the employer pays the fee and my study hours. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only with a signed offer showing written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel, keeping my call job until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a paid trial would tell me more than a leaflet. I will not damage my back for a job that pays less after the bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try in stockroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the parcel label and compare it with the shelf position while someone watches. If the boxes are too heavy, I would not call the role suitable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What transport would you compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen (my partner) and I would compare his unloading rota with mine. If both of us needed the same bus at the same time, we would check the cost of another route before signing.

say: I’d seek a **supervised paid trial** for posted stockroom work.
I’d insist on **safe lifting** before accepting that role.
think: I think I could learn **parcel checks** beside a worker.
I know **2031 AI** reaches records before later robots lift boxes.
do: Try **supervised paid stockroom shift** only for posted paid vacancy with safe lifting.
Take **required safety course** only with employer-paid fees and study hours for that role.
Move after 2031 on **signed written terms** covering weekly bills after travel; compare both rotas and alternative-route cost before signing.
feel: **Anxious**, but ready to inspect safe paid work.
S3.quote: I will not damage my back for a job that pays less after the bus fare.
fieldNote: The **trial** requires a posted paid role and safe lifting.
The **course** is only worthwhile when fees and study time are paid.
Both work rotas affect **transport cost** before an offer is signed.

steps.text: Try supervised paid stockroom trial only for posted opening with safe lifting
Take required safety course for posted paid stockroom opening only with funded fees and paid study
Move on signed written bill-covering weekly wages/hours after checking both rotas, bus and alternate-route cost

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us ten years, but I would not call that a retirement plan. I would keep asking how many paid order shifts are on each yearly rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may still need a wage at 68; Owen and I have not checked what money would come in if I stopped. Full thinking AI could take my calls in 2036, and robots around 2039 are later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid order calls and write our actual wages and bills beside what little we have saved. If I still need work after 2036 and my call hours fall, I’d move to a posted paid desk role only on a signed offer whose written weekly wages and hours cover bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money even with ten years. Age alone will not pay for groceries at 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check retirement money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Owen (my partner) to help me check the real income and bills before we decide any retirement date. I would not assume a pension amount before seeing it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children should not have to build our plan for us. If they offered help, I would listen, but I would not put it in the budget now.

say: I’d ask for **yearly paid-order rotas** as long as the centre still takes calls.
I’d say **ten years** is no retirement guarantee.
think: I think I may **need wages** at 68 if our bills remain high.
I cannot assume **pension money** without written figures.
do: Keep **paid order calls** and compare real wages, bills and savings in 2026.
Move to **posted paid desk work** if hours fall and wages remain needed, only on signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours.
feel: **Anxious** about household income despite more time.
S4.quote: Age alone will not pay for groceries at 68.
fieldNote: Her **retirement date** depends on checked money, not an assumed pension.
The **thin reserve** keeps the decade scenario financially tense.
Adult children’s **help is unpromised** and outside the budget.

steps.text: Keep taking paid order calls and compare real wages, bills and savings
Move if wages needed/hours cut: posted desk, signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A machine could handle routine order calls before I become steady at them, and Owen’s part-time wage would not cover our bills. I would need written notice, a real posted paid job close enough to reach, and teaching during paid hours if a new role requires it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I trust a person who shows me the job beside them. A folder of screens at home would not teach me how a wrong parcel feels in my hands.

headlineQuote: A folder of screens at home would not teach me how a wrong parcel feels in my hands.
portrait: At **58**, Beth is a junior order agent still learning after secondary school.
She and Owen have **grown children**, low pay and less than one month of expenses saved.
With **few nearby jobs**, she needs a real posted opening before changing work.
She **never uses AI** and prefers practical teaching beside another worker.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take routine order calls before she becomes secure in the job.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, reachable posted work and paid role-required teaching would help.
